div.head: Editorial Principles
div.p: This page records the editorial decisions taken in the making of eLiebermann, and the methods by which its texts have been transcribed, checked and encoded. It is revised as the work proceeds. For an account of the project, of Felix Liebermann and his Gesetze, and of how to cite eLiebermann, see About.

div.head: General
Aims and scope
div.p: eLiebermann has been built from spreadsheets and transcriptions compiled over a number of years for the editor's research on the language and composition of the early English laws, and its structure, corrections and indexing reflect the questions that this research has asked of the texts. It is offered here in the hope that it may be of wider use to others working on the laws and their language.

The Lawcodes Database is concerned principally with the Old English laws issued before 1066, and its record of these codes is the most complete. It also reproduces the majority of the other legal and quasi-legal texts that Liebermann prints, including some post-Conquest codes and compilations. The Legal Dictionary is an edition of the whole of Liebermann's Wörterbuch.
div.head: Liebermann and beyond
div.p: The project takes its name from Felix Liebermann, and his Gesetze der Angelsachsen is its foundation: his texts, his German translation, his apparatus and his clause divisions are the frame to which everything else is fitted.

The project aims, however, to be more than a digital reproduction of the Gesetze. It gathers beside Liebermann's text the editions and translations of later scholars, where these can be reproduced; it directs readers by page number to more recent editions of Liebermann's clauses; it organises and corrects the texts, checking them against the printed volumes and against Liebermann's own textual notes and corrections; it records cross-references between clauses drawn from Liebermann's margins and from the scholarship of the following century; and it adds a subject index of the laws that is the editor's own. Where the site corrects or adds to Liebermann, this is noted.
div.head: The base text
div.p: Liebermann's text is reproduced as he printed it, with his sigla, his numbering and his typography. Every dictionary entry and every lawcode clause page is linked to its page in a scan of the printed volume (on archive.org), so that any reading may be verified against the original.
div.head: Method
div.p: The editorial work combines the editor's transcriptions, corrections and scholarship with machine-assisted transcription, collation and encoding.

Every dictionary entry and every lawcode clause is a separate file in TEI XML, the international standard for scholarly digital editions (Text Encoding Initiative, P5). All the project's text and data are kept under version control in a Git repository, in which every addition or correction, whether made by hand or by script, is proposed as a separate, documented change and published only after review. Errors may be reported, and new entries suggested, through Make a suggestion or the Suggest a change link at the foot of each entry.

div.head: The Legal Dictionary
Transcription and collation
div.p: Every dictionary entry has been transcribed twice, independently. The project team keyed all entries by hand; a second transcription was made in 2026 from page images of the Wörterbuch by Claude, a large language model developed by Anthropic. The two transcriptions have been collated entry by entry and word by word. Each disagreement is classified (a slip in one transcription or the other, a difference of typography only, or a different division between entries) and, where it cannot be settled from the transcriptions alone, is checked by the editor against the printed volume. A report of each collation, and a running list of readings still to be checked against the print, are kept with the project's data.
div.head: Typography
div.p: Liebermann's typography carries meaning: roman type is the language of the laws; italic is Liebermann's German and his grammatical commentary; bold marks headwords; and a superscript L or F marks a Latin or French word. This system is preserved in the transcriptions, and has occasionally been regularised where Liebermann's own practice is inconsistent. Page breaks are recorded, so that each entry is linked to its page in the printed volume.
div.head: Abbreviations, technical terms and conventional signs
div.p: Liebermann's Wörterbuch relies on a dense system of abbreviations, grammatical terms and conventional signs, which Liebermann nowhere sets out in full. The list of Grammatical Terms and Abbreviations, and the pop-ups drawn from it throughout the dictionary, are the editor's reconstruction of that system. Each item gives (i) the German form as Liebermann wrote it out, or as he would have written it out; (ii) the modern standard German equivalent, where the spelling or the word itself has since changed; and (iii) an English translation; with notes where needed.

Where Liebermann gives no expansion, the meaning has been inferred from his usage. Every one of the c. 500 abbreviations (639 forms in all) has been checked against its occurrences across the entries. An exclamation mark after a quoted form, for example, which Liebermann does not explain, is taken to mean sic, since it appears where a manuscript has an unexpected or incorrect form (an accusative ending, say, where a dative would be expected).

Liebermann is not wholly consistent in either his terminology or his abbreviations. One term may appear in more than one abbreviated form, and one abbreviation may serve for more than one term: sbj stands for "subject" in the grammatical notes but for "subjunctive" in the Old French entries. Some expansions offered here are therefore necessarily provisional. The list is meant as an aid to Liebermann's technical and explanatory vocabulary, not as a glossary of the ordinary German of his definitions, whose words are accordingly not linked. Corrections are welcome through Make a suggestion.

Law-code sigla, manuscript sigla and grammatical abbreviations within an entry are identified automatically in the first instance, by longest match against the authority lists compiled by the editor, and linked to their expansions. In those frequent cases where Liebermann further shortens his abbreviations or citations and automatic linking is not possible, the editor has created the relevant links. Finding and correcting missing or incorrect links is an ongoing process; corrections are welcome via Make a suggestion.
div.head: Citations of the laws
div.p: Each citation of a law in an entry is normalised to a standard key (law code and clause number, following the usual scholarly form of citation) and linked to that clause in the Lawcodes Database.
div.head: Authors and works cited
div.p: Liebermann prints no bibliography, and cites modern scholarship and editions by short title. The full citations on the list of Authors and Works Cited have been reconstructed by the editor from those short titles, from the two brief lists of works in the Gesetze (I, p. LIV; II.2, p. 262), and from the editions current when he wrote. Where Liebermann cites a primary source without naming an edition, the edition he most probably used is given. These identifications are marked as provisional until they can be checked against the editions themselves.
div.head: Cross-reference and spelling entries
div.p: Liebermann's own cross-references between entries (s. WORD) are given as links. An entry that serves only to send the reader to another headword is shown with the headword or headwords to which it refers, without the further apparatus of a full entry. Headwords that record orthographic variation rather than a distinct word (for example aa for ā) are marked as spelling entries.
div.head: Editorial corrections
div.p: Where Liebermann's printed entry is corrected (where, for example, it refers the reader to a headword that does not exist, or to an incorrect spelling), the change is explained in an Editor's note on the entry page.
div.head: Other dictionaries
div.p: Where possible, Old English headwords are linked to the corresponding entries in the Bosworth–Toller Anglo-Saxon Dictionary, the Dictionary of Old English, and/or Wiktionary. These links are the work of the project team and are not yet complete. The links to Bosworth–Toller were first made by a semi-automated process, and some may be erroneous until checked and corrected by the editor.

div.head: The Lawcodes Database
Compilation
div.p: The database is compiled in a master spreadsheet of more than fifty fields for each clause, from which the clause files are generated by script. For every clause the spreadsheet records at least Liebermann's text of each manuscript he prints, identified by his siglum, with his page number; his German translation; and an English rendering of his German.
div.head: Clause division
div.p: Liebermann's division of the laws into clauses is followed throughout, so that every citation of the form used by Liebermann and by the scholarship that depends on him leads to a single clause. The texts of later editions are divided at Liebermann's clause breaks, including those printed by their editors as continuous prose. Where a later editor divides a clause more finely, the clause is kept whole and the editor's divisions are marked within it by that editor's own numbers.
div.head: Manuscripts
div.p: Every text is identified by the manuscript from which it is taken, under Liebermann's siglum. Where Liebermann prints the text from more than one manuscript, his main text (taken to be that in his leftmost column) is given first.
div.head: Later editions
div.p: The texts and translations of later editions are entered with their page references, and are in the process of being re-checked against the printed books.
div.head: Translations
div.p: Liebermann's German translation is accompanied by a close, semi-literal English rendering, made with the assistance of a large language model (Claude, developed by Anthropic, 2026) and labelled as such on every clause page. It is intended as a crib to Liebermann's German; it is not a new translation of the Old English, and should not be quoted as one. The editor has corrected some of its more egregious misprisions where these have been noticed, but it has not been systematically revised, and should be used with caution. The translations of modern editors follow, each attributed.
div.head: Liebermann's notes
div.p: Liebermann's textual notes and his commentary (the Erklärungen of volume III) are given in the form of notes linked to his German translation, as printed. Each is accompanied by an English rendering. These notes are hidden by default, to be shown clause by clause. Note that much of this commentary, and many of the legal comparisons Liebermann draws, have been superseded by later scholarship.
div.head: Cross-references between clauses
div.p: The early English legal corpus contains many laws that repeat or draw upon earlier laws, and certain "early" laws are in fact later compositions attributed to earlier kings. A record of the similarities between clauses offers a means of tracing these features of legislative composition. Liebermann's marginal cross-references have accordingly been transcribed from the page images of volume I, and the cross-references and comparisons of later scholars collected from their studies, editions, footnotes and tables of sources. Each is given with its source and page, and is linked in both directions. The wording on each clause page distinguishes the references made at that clause from those made at other clauses that point to it. The record is not yet complete, and suggestions for additional links are welcome.
div.head: Subject index
div.p: Every clause has been read and indexed by the offences, people, places and other matters with which it deals. The index was made for this project and is independent of Liebermann's Rechts- und Sachglossar (volume II, part 2).
div.head: Record of checking
div.p: Checking is recorded clause by clause: the foot of each clause page states what has been checked, and against which page of which book. This work is ongoing, and the record on each clause will note when a final check has been made by a member of the project team.
